Fit a Variable Length Markov Chain with Covariates (COVLMC)

Source: R/covlmc.R
covlmc.default.Rd

This function fits a Variable Length Markov Chain with covariates (COVLMC) to a discrete time series coupled with a time series of covariates.

Usage

# Default S3 method
covlmc(
  x,
  covariate,
  alpha = 0.05,
  min_size = 5L,
  max_depth = 100L,
  keep_data = TRUE,
  control = covlmc_control(...),
  ...
)

Arguments

x

a numeric, character, factor or logical vector

covariate

a data frame of covariates, with one row per observation of x, at least one column and no missing values.

alpha

number in (0,1] (default: 0.05) cut off value in the pruning phase (in quantile scale).

min_size

number >= 1 (default: 5). Tune the minimum number of observations for a context in the growing phase of the context tree (see below for details).

max_depth

integer >= 0 (default: 100). Longest context considered in the growing phase of the context tree.

keep_data

logical (defaults to TRUE). If TRUE, the original data are stored in the resulting object to enable post-pruning (see prune.covlmc()).

control

a list with control parameters, see covlmc_control().

...

arguments passed to covlmc_control().

Value

a fitted VLMC with covariates, an object of class covlmc.

Details

The model is built using the algorithm described in Zanin Zambom et al. As for the vlmc() approach, the algorithm builds first a context tree (see ctx_tree()). The min_size parameter is used to compute the actual number of observations per context in the growing phase of the tree. It is computed as min_size*(1+p*d)*(s-1) where d is the length of the context (a.k.a. the depth in the tree), s is the number of states and p is the number of parameters associated with one time step of the covariates (one per numerical or logical covariate, and the number of levels minus one per factor). This corresponds to ensuring min_size observations per parameter of the logistic regression during the estimation phase.

Then logistic models are fitted in the leaves of the tree: the goal of each logistic model is to estimate the conditional distribution of the next state of the time series given the context (the recent past of the time series) and delayed versions of the covariates. A pruning strategy is used to simplify the models (mainly to reduce the time window associated with the covariates) and the tree itself.

Parameters specified by control are used to fine-tune the behaviour of the algorithm.

Logistic models

By default, covlmc uses two different computing engines for logistic models:

  • when the time series has only two states, covlmc uses stats::glm() with the binomial family (stats::binomial());

  • when the time series has at least three states, covlmc uses VGAM::vglm() with the multinomial family (VGAM::multinomial()).

It is possible to replace stats::glm() and VGAM::vglm() with nnet::multinom() by setting the global option mixvlmc.predictive to "multinom" (the default value is "glm"). The engines estimate the same models, but their results are not always identical:

  • stats::glm() and VGAM::vglm() use iteratively reweighted least squares while nnet::multinom() uses a quasi-Newton optimisation. When the data of a context are (almost) separable, for instance when a value of a covariate determines the next state, the maximum likelihood coefficients are infinite and the engines stop at different (large) values. The likelihoods remain very close, but the coefficients can be quite different and a likelihood ratio test whose p-value is close to alpha can lead to different decisions, and thus to different models.

  • stats::glm() and VGAM::vglm() report a warning when they do not converge in mixvlmc.maxit iterations (see mixvlmc-package), while nnet::multinom() does not.

  • the states that never follow a context in the data are ignored by the model of this context, which gives them a zero probability and has fewer coefficients. Similarly, levels of factor covariates absent from the data of a context are ignored: VGAM::vglm() reports no coefficient for them while stats::glm() and nnet::multinom() report a zero coefficient (for instance in the text format of draw.covlmc(); the LaTeX format shows zero coefficients for all the engines).

The engine used to estimate a COVLMC is recorded in the model: it is also used to estimate the new logistic models needed by prune.covlmc(), even if the option has been changed in between (with a warning).

The number of parameters of a COVLMC, used by stats::AIC() and stats::BIC(), counts the coefficients of the covariates actually estimated by the engine (as a consequence of the last point of the list above) and all the intercepts: it does not depend on the engine (see the "Number of parameters" section of loglikelihood.covlmc()).

References

  • Bühlmann, P. and Wyner, A. J. (1999), "Variable length Markov chains." Ann. Statist. 27 (2) 480-513 doi:10.1214/aos/1018031204

  • Zanin Zambom, A., Kim, S. and Lopes Garcia, N. (2022), "Variable length Markov chain with exogenous covariates." J. Time Ser. Anal., 43 (2) 312-328 doi:10.1111/jtsa.12615

See also

cutoff.covlmc() and prune.covlmc() for post-pruning, tune_covlmc() for automatic model selection.

Examples

pc <- powerconsumption[powerconsumption$week == 5, ]
rdts <- cut(pc$active_power, breaks = c(0, quantile(pc$active_power,
  probs = c(1 / 3, 2 / 3, 1)
)))
rdts_cov <- data.frame(day_night = (pc$hour >= 7 & pc$hour <= 17))
m_cov <- covlmc(rdts, rdts_cov, min_size = 15)
draw(m_cov)
#> ▪
#> ├─ (0,0.556] ([ -2.885 • 1.237
#> │               -4.185 • -15.4 ])
#> ├─ (0.556,1.78] (0.1012, 0.7827, 0.1161)
#> └─ (1.78,7.54] (0.002976, 0.122, 0.875)
withr::with_options(
  list(mixvlmc.predictive = "multinom"),
  m_cov_nnet <- covlmc(rdts, rdts_cov, min_size = 15)
)
draw(m_cov_nnet)
#> ▪
#> ├─ (0,0.556] ([ -2.885 • 1.237 
#> │               -4.185 • -7.944 ])
#> ├─ (0.556,1.78] (0.1012, 0.7827, 0.1161)
#> └─ (1.78,7.54] (0.002976, 0.122, 0.875)
